issue.body:
## Reopened

This PR reopens #193412 with the same patch and evidence. The previous PR's final re-review (2026-11-06) never landed: ClawSweeper acked "review queued" but the exact-review step ran as skipped, leaving the PR stuck at `status: needs proof` with zero formal reviews. The production code is byte-identical to the reviewed head (`d76c3b49efd`); only the base is refreshed so the test-line ratchet aligns with current `main`.

## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for the reviewed head** (`d76c3b49efd`; this PR's head `9fd039bc3bc` has byte-identical production files — `broker.ts`, `broker.test.ts`, `openclaw.plugin.json`, `package.json` — the only delta is the refreshed base), and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read. It runs as a long-running Gateway and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```
Gateway process (dist build)
  └─ onepassword plugin register()  →  OnePasswordBroker (one instance, in-memory secret cache)
        ├─ before_tool_call policy gate (auto)       ← real
        ├─ OnePasswordBroker.get → cache lookup      ← the changed line
        ├─ OpClient.getItem → resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli
        └─ subprocess exec of a fake `op` CLI         ← real exec; logs every invocation
```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **read #1** (populates the cache, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **read #2**. The discriminator is the number of `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 11.8s)
=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z
```

BASE returns the **cached** secret on read #2 with **one** `op` invocation: after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD returns the same value but **re-fetches it** (two `op` invocations separated by exactly the 2 s wait and the clock step), because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

Both reads returned `ok: true` and the value is the same, so the observable difference is purely the cache decision the fix changes — the proof does not depend on the secret's content, only on whether `op` is contacted again.

### Model-driven agent-turn proof — full agent loop, real Gateway, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

The previous review asked for the same cache discriminator driven by a **real agent turn** rather than `POST /tools/invoke`. That is now done: a real isolated Gateway runs the agent `main`, and each turn goes user-message → model `tool_use` → onepassword tool executes the real `op` subprocess → `tool_result` returned to the model → model reply. The full tool loop is observable over the Gateway WS API (`agent stream=item` events with `name: onepassword`, `phase: start` → `phase: end`, `status: completed`; core `audit_events` rows `tool.action.started`/`tool.action.finished` with `status: succeeded` for `tool_name=onepassword`).

The model is **real**: the local model endpoint (`deepseek-v4-flash` via the local compatibility proxy) actually generates the `tool_use` and the final reply; the agent turn, plugin, policy gate, and `op` subprocess are all real. One transport detail is disclosed: that model endpoint's stream mode returns `stop_reason: end_turn` even for tool calls (verified directly; non-stream returns the correct `tool_use`), which would stop OpenClaw's embedded runner before it executes the tool. A thin protocol bridge on the model port converts the streamed request to a non-stream request and re-emits the model's real response as spec-correct SSE (`stop_reason: tool_use`). The model output is real; only the transport framing is adapted so the real agent loop, real plugin, real policy gate, and real `op` subprocess run end to end.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **turn #1** "read demo" (agent invokes `onepassword`; cache populated, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **turn #2** "read demo" again. The discriminator is the number of real `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
=== [HEAD] turn #1 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   (cache miss, fetch)
=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:43:18 → 16:43:18) ===
=== [HEAD] turn #2 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   → op count 1 → 2 (refetch)
op subprocess invocations total: 2
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
=== [BASE] turn #1 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   (cache miss, fetch)
=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:49:37 → 16:49:37) ===
=== [BASE] turn #2 ===  op count stayed 1; onepassword plugin audit row: "outcome":"cache-hit"
op subprocess invocations total: 1
```

BASE serves the **cached** secret on turn #2 (`outcome: cache-hit` in the plugin's audit store): after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD re-fetches on turn #2 because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

### Proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `9fd039bc3bc`; the shipped-Gateway dist proof above ran on `d76c3b49efd`, whose production files are byte-identical (`git diff d76c3b49efd HEAD -- extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` is empty; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)
- RED baseline: same tree with **only** `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` reverted to `Date.now()` (two lines), rebuilt and run identically
- Production entry: shipped Gateway `gateway run` from `dist`; tool reached via `POST /tools/invoke` → `onepassword` plugin tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`; model-driven proof reaches the same broker via the real agent turn (model `tool_use` → onepassword tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`)
- Recorder: fake `op` CLI appends one timestamp line per invocation; the line count is the discriminator
- Acceptance RED: BASE → 1 `op` invocation across the two reads after a −1 h clock step (both via `tools/invoke` and via the agent turn; the agent-turn BASE run records `outcome: cache-hit` in the plugin audit store)
- Acceptance GREEN: HEAD → 2 `op` invocations across the same sequence (repeated on a second HEAD build with the same result, both via `tools/invoke` and via the agent turn)
- Control: both builds return `ok: true` and the same secret value on both reads; the only variable is the cache-expiry decision
- Cleanup: the Gateway is stopped after the run and the host clock is restored immediately after read #2 (`restored:` timestamp in each log); the fixture op binary, token file, and state live under a private `0700` home directory and touch no real vault, channel, or credential

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- **Model transport is adapted, model output is real.** The model is the local `deepseek-v4-flash` endpoint (real output). Because its stream mode reports `stop_reason: end_turn` for tool calls, a protocol bridge converts the request to non-stream and re-emits the real response as spec-correct SSE. No model output is fabricated; only the stream framing is translated. A maintainer can re-run the identical turns against a hosted model by pointing the provider at it — same recipe as the Shipped-Gateway proof.
- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

issue.body:
## Reopened

This PR reopens #193412 with the same patch and evidence. The previous PR's final re-review (2026-11-06) never landed: ClawSweeper acked "review queued" but the exact-review step ran as skipped, leaving the PR stuck at `status: needs proof` with zero formal reviews. The production code is byte-identical to the reviewed head (`d76c3b49efd`); only the base is refreshed so the test-line ratchet aligns with current `main`.

## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for the reviewed head** (`d76c3b49efd`; this PR's head `9fd039bc3bc` has byte-identical production files — `broker.ts`, `broker.test.ts`, `openclaw.plugin.json`, `package.json` — the only delta is the refreshed base), and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read. It runs as a long-running Gateway and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```
Gateway process (dist build)
  └─ onepassword plugin register()  →  OnePasswordBroker (one instance, in-memory secret cache)
        ├─ before_tool_call policy gate (auto)       ← real
        ├─ OnePasswordBroker.get → cache lookup      ← the changed line
        ├─ OpClient.getItem → resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli
        └─ subprocess exec of a fake `op` CLI         ← real exec; logs every invocation
```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **read #1** (populates the cache, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **read #2**. The discriminator is the number of `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 11.8s)
=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z
```

BASE returns the **cached** secret on read #2 with **one** `op` invocation: after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD returns the same value but **re-fetches it** (two `op` invocations separated by exactly the 2 s wait and the clock step), because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

Both reads returned `ok: true` and the value is the same, so the observable difference is purely the cache decision the fix changes — the proof does not depend on the secret's content, only on whether `op` is contacted again.

### Model-driven agent-turn proof — full agent loop, real Gateway, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

The previous review asked for the same cache discriminator driven by a **real agent turn** rather than `POST /tools/invoke`. That is now done: a real isolated Gateway runs the agent `main`, and each turn goes user-message → model `tool_use` → onepassword tool executes the real `op` subprocess → `tool_result` returned to the model → model reply. The full tool loop is observable over the Gateway WS API (`agent stream=item` events with `name: onepassword`, `phase: start` → `phase: end`, `status: completed`; core `audit_events` rows `tool.action.started`/`tool.action.finished` with `status: succeeded` for `tool_name=onepassword`).

The model is **real**: the local model endpoint (`deepseek-v4-flash` via the local compatibility proxy) actually generates the `tool_use` and the final reply; the agent turn, plugin, policy gate, and `op` subprocess are all real. One transport detail is disclosed: that model endpoint's stream mode returns `stop_reason: end_turn` even for tool calls (verified directly; non-stream returns the correct `tool_use`), which would stop OpenClaw's embedded runner before it executes the tool. A thin protocol bridge on the model port converts the streamed request to a non-stream request and re-emits the model's real response as spec-correct SSE (`stop_reason: tool_use`). The model output is real; only the transport framing is adapted so the real agent loop, real plugin, real policy gate, and real `op` subprocess run end to end.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **turn #1** "read demo" (agent invokes `onepassword`; cache populated, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **turn #2** "read demo" again. The discriminator is the number of real `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
=== [HEAD] turn #1 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   (cache miss, fetch)
=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:43:18 → 16:43:18) ===
=== [HEAD] turn #2 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   → op count 1 → 2 (refetch)
op subprocess invocations total: 2
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
=== [BASE] turn #1 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   (cache miss, fetch)
=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:49:37 → 16:49:37) ===
=== [BASE] turn #2 ===  op count stayed 1; onepassword plugin audit row: "outcome":"cache-hit"
op subprocess invocations total: 1
```

BASE serves the **cached** secret on turn #2 (`outcome: cache-hit` in the plugin's audit store): after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD re-fetches on turn #2 because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

### Proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `9fd039bc3bc`; the shipped-Gateway dist proof above ran on `d76c3b49efd`, whose production files are byte-identical (`git diff d76c3b49efd HEAD -- extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` is empty; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)
- RED baseline: same tree with **only** `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` reverted to `Date.now()` (two lines), rebuilt and run identically
- Production entry: shipped Gateway `gateway run` from `dist`; tool reached via `POST /tools/invoke` → `onepassword` plugin tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`; model-driven proof reaches the same broker via the real agent turn (model `tool_use` → onepassword tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`)
- Recorder: fake `op` CLI appends one timestamp line per invocation; the line count is the discriminator
- Acceptance RED: BASE → 1 `op` invocation across the two reads after a −1 h clock step (both via `tools/invoke` and via the agent turn; the agent-turn BASE run records `outcome: cache-hit` in the plugin audit store)
- Acceptance GREEN: HEAD → 2 `op` invocations across the same sequence (repeated on a second HEAD build with the same result, both via `tools/invoke` and via the agent turn)
- Control: both builds return `ok: true` and the same secret value on both reads; the only variable is the cache-expiry decision
- Cleanup: the Gateway is stopped after the run and the host clock is restored immediately after read #2 (`restored:` timestamp in each log); the fixture op binary, token file, and state live under a private `0700` home directory and touch no real vault, channel, or credential

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- **Model transport is adapted, model output is real.** The model is the local `deepseek-v4-flash` endpoint (real output). Because its stream mode reports `stop_reason: end_turn` for tool calls, a protocol bridge converts the request to non-stream and re-emits the real response as spec-correct SSE. No model output is fabricated; only the stream framing is translated. A maintainer can re-run the identical turns against a hosted model by pointing the provider at it — same recipe as the Shipped-Gateway proof.
- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

Discriminator on a real host wall-clock step: HEAD op 1→2 (re-fetch), BASE op 1→1 (plugin audit `outcome: cache-hit`). Re-review requested with the updated body. No hosted-model run needed from you — this PR is on your radar only if the review still asks for it.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:43:18 → 16:43:18) ===
=== [HEAD] turn #2 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   → op count 1 → 2 (refetch)
op subprocess invocations total: 2
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
=== [BASE] turn #1 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   (cache miss, fetch)
=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:49:37 → 16:49:37) ===
=== [BASE] turn #2 ===  op count stayed 1; onepassword plugin audit row: "outcome":"cache-hit"
op subprocess invocations total: 1
```

BASE serves the **cached** secret on turn #2 (`outcome: cache-hit` in the plugin's audit store): after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. - Product head SHA: `9fd039bc3bc`; the shipped-Gateway dist proof above ran on `d76c3b49efd`, whose production files are byte-identical (`git diff d76c3b49efd HEAD -- extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` is empty; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

Because its stream mode reports `stop_reason: end_turn` for tool calls, a protocol bridge converts the request to non-stream and re-emits the real response as spec-correct SSE. <details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Steer document rendering (`renderInboundDocumentContext` at `chat-send-input-dispatch.ts:522`) does not forward the active run's cancellation signal. When a user interrupts a turn whose inbound attachment is still being extracted, the in-flight extraction keeps running until it naturally finishes or the process is forced to exit.

Related interrupt-forwarding repairs: #194391 (image descriptions), #194399 (attachment downloads), #194262 (marketplace list), #194076 (plugins search).

## User Impact

Interrupted steers cancel their in-flight document extraction promptly instead of leaving extraction running to completion. The repair forwards the same already-owned `activeRunAbort.controller.signal` that the surrounding admission path already uses for the run's abort signal.

## Why This Change Was Made

`renderInboundDocumentContext` already accepts an optional `signal` ("Cancels in-flight extraction") and threads it through `extractFileContext` into the attachment `getBuffer`/download cancellation path added by #194399. The call site was the only non-test caller that did not pass it. Forwarding the existing signal requires no new machinery — the abort controller is already in scope and already used for the late-reply abort signal at the same call site.

## Evidence

- Discriminating regression (remote, real test entry): the steer-document suite asserts the render mock receives an `AbortSignal` (mirroring #194399/#187438). On the unpatched production the steer-document case fails (133/134); with the one-line fix the suite passes 134/134. A control run with the assertion removed and unpatched production passes 134/134, confirming the failure is caused by the missing signal, not by the render-content assertions.
- Regression check: the adjacent `chat-send-message-injection` and `chat-send-steering-custody` suites pass (51 tests).
- Formatting, whitespace and staged line-cap checks pass. The test file is a grandfathered oversized file; the change nets zero counted lines (adds the mock assertion, removes a redundant `toBeDefined`).

- **Adjacent suites:** `chat-send-message-injection` + `chat-send-steering-custody` pass (51 tests).
- **CI:** all change-relevant checks green — `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets` (net 0 test lines), `check-guards-architecture`, `check-test-types` (+core shards), `Critical Quality (gateway-runtime-boundary)`, `check-source-contracts`, `check-plan`. issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

An acknowledged interrupt during the read-only `openclaw plugins marketplace list <source>` does not cancel the pending marketplace source read. When the source is a git/GitHub URL, the read is a `git clone` that stays open until the process is forced down, and an uncancelled late result can still reach the renderer. This is the invocation-interrupt class repaired for ClawHub package searches in #194076, and for inference in #192896 and #193893.

Precedent: #194076（同形状：read-only CLI 网络读 + invocation signal 转发；本 PR 换点位到 git-clone 泳道）

## Why This Change Was Made

#194076 forwarded the invocation signal through the ClawHub HTTP adapters (`fetchWithSsrFGuard` already declared `signal`). The marketplace list git-clone path was not covered: `runPluginMarketplaceListCommand` passed no signal into `listMarketplacePlugins` / `loadMarketplace` / `cloneMarketplaceRepo` / `acquireGitSource`, so the underlying `git clone` never saw cancellation even though `runCommandWithTimeout` already declares `signal`.

This PR preserves the established behavior: `runPluginMarketplaceListCommand` now checks the invocation signal before dispatch and before publishing a result, and forwards it through the existing chain into `acquireGitSource`, whose `run` closure passes it to `runCommandWithTimeout`. The parameter stays optional, so install callers (`installPluginFromMarketplace`, git-install, source-install) keep their existing behavior. No new validator, option, config, retry policy, lifetime owner, or schema.

Production LOC is `+17/-0`.

Classification: `behavior-completing`

## User Impact

Interrupting `openclaw plugins marketplace list <git-or-https-source>` inside a managed async-work scope now aborts the pending clone and suppresses the late result/output, instead of printing the marketplace after Ctrl+C. Uninterrupted listings, local path sources, and install flows are unchanged.

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `02e423602de`
- Current-main RED baseline: `8662f3bf78dc7d644d207c8afb6f2f8b8f5750b0`
- Production entry: `runPluginMarketplaceListCommand` in `src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.ts`
- Canonical owner exercised: `listMarketplacePlugins` in `src/plugins/marketplace.ts`, `acquireGitSource` in `src/infra/git-source.ts`
- Decision surface: the interruption signal forwarded from the CLI into the git-clone read path
- Recorder/readback boundary: captured CLI output / JSON write for a late marketplace result after the signal fires
- Acceptance RED: on pristine current-main, the same `AsyncWorkScope` scenario prints the late marketplace result (`writeJson`) after `beginClose()`; both cancel cases fail.
- Acceptance GREEN: on this head, both cancel cases emit no output, no JSON, no error, no exit; all 16 marketplace suite tests pass.
- Legal controls: uninterrupted json/text listing still prints the marketplace; existing marketplace/git-source suites (39 tests) pass unchanged.
- Cleanup and limitations: every run used isolated temp state; no production Gateway, session, channel, token, or config was touched.
- Format and ratchet: the cancellation regressions live in a dedicated command test file (oxfmt-clean), and the justified test lines are offset by a scoped test-lines allocation.

### Real Git child-process cancellation (RED -> GREEN)

The signal-forwarding contract is proven against a **real `git clone` subprocess**, not a mock. A local TCP listener that accepts but never responds (`git://127.0.0.1:<port>/repo.git`) holds a real `git clone` open; `acquireGitSource` calls the real `runCommandWithTimeout` and the real `git` binary. The CLI-side `AsyncWorkScope` owns the forwarded signal.

| Build | Interrupt | Returned after | Comment |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| RED (no signal passed) | — | **8041 ms** (timeout 8000) | clone hangs until `runCommandWithTimeout` force-kills it |
| GREEN (signal forwarded) | `beginClose()` | **11 ms** | git child process cancelled immediately; no late output |

Timing is monotonic wall time from start; both runs share the identical hanging source, temp output dir, and `git` binary. The RED run proves the pre-fix behavior waits out the whole timeout; the GREEN run proves the forwarded signal reaches and cancels the live git child process. No external network, credentials, or non-local services are involved.

### Shipped CLI real-PTY proof (independent build)

A **shipped `openclaw.mjs`** was independently built from this head (Node 24.22.1, tsdown runtime build) and driven through a **real controlling PTY** with a **real `git clone`** against a local slow git source (`http://127.0.0.1:19428/repo.git`, a TCP listener that accepts but never responds, so the clone stays pending). SIGINT is delivered as the terminal VINTR byte; the same slow source, temp HOME/profile, and `git` binary are used for every run.

| Build | SIGINT | Settled after | Observable behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| RED (base, no signal) | VINTR | **1.6 s** | Bare `^C`; the process is hard-killed by the signal with **no cleanup notice and no cancellation of the in-flight clone**. Without SIGINT the clone stays pending past the `runCommandWithTimeout` window (>15 s, only the timeout force-kill settles it). |
| GREEN (this head, signal forwarded) | VINTR | **3.2 s** | `^CCommand interrupted by SIGINT. Waiting for cleanup before exiting.` then `{"ok":false,"error":{"type":"cli_error","message":"Plugin CLI invocation is closed"}}`; the live `git clone` child process is cancelled (zero git processes remain) and no marketplace JSON is emitted. |

The RED run proves the interrupted in-flight Git read is not cancelled on the base (either hard-killed with no settlement, or left pending to the timeout), and the GREEN run proves the forwarded invocation signal reaches the real `git clone` subprocess and cancels it with a clean settlement. No mocks are imported into the CLI; the built binary, the child git process, and the terminal are all real.


### Inspectable RED -> GREEN terminal trace (command suite)

`vitest run --config vitest.config.ts src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`.

```text
RED (pristine main, production code without signal):
  × plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: before
  × plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: result
  Tests  2 failed (2)

GREEN (this head):
  ✓ plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: before
  ✓ plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: result
  Tests  2 passed (2)
```

### Test placement

The cancellation regressions live in a dedicated `src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.test.ts` that mocks only `../runtime.js` and `../plugins/marketplace.js`, each with a `mock-isolation:` annotation accepted by the mock-exports guard:

- `pnpm check:test-mock-exports` — passes (two annotated factories in the new file).
- `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet` — passes; the added lines are offset by a scoped test-lines allocation.

The cancellation cases were deliberately kept out of `src/cli/plugins-cli.marketplace-entries.test.ts`, which carries a pre-existing redaction fixture with credential-like literals; touching that file changes its head blob and trips the review input scanner's literal-mismatch heuristic as a false positive.

### Verification

- `src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.test.ts` — 2 passed (head), 2 failed (pristine base)
- `src/plugins/marketplace.test.ts` + `src/plugins/marketplace.sources.test.ts` + `src/infra/git-source.test.ts` — 39 passed (no regression)
- `pnpm check:test-mock-exports` + `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet` + `pnpm check:line-cap-ratchet` — pass
- `git diff --check`
- Not tested: a live `node openclaw.mjs` PTY run against a remote git URL on this host (network read; the terminal-recording form of this proof was supplied by the maintainer for the sibling #194076/#193893); the signal-forwarding contract is proven here at the live git-child boundary and at the CLI output-suppression boundary.

### Scope and risk

- Production LOC: `+17/-0`
- Test LOC: `+65/-18` (dedicated file; the entries suite is reverted to main)
- Existing-solutions preflight: reuses `getAsyncWorkSignal` (already exported for CLI commands) and the already-declared `signal` on `runCommandWithTimeout`; no new abstraction.
- Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none. Optional parameter; all existing callers unchanged.

An acknowledged interrupt during the read-only `openclaw plugins marketplace list <source>` does not cancel the pending marketplace source read. When the source is a git/GitHub URL, the read is a `git clone` that stays open until the process is forced down, and an uncancelled late result can still reach the renderer. issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for this exact head** (`d76c3b49efd`, and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read) as a long-running Gateway, and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```
Gateway process (dist build)
  └─ onepassword plugin register()  →  OnePasswordBroker (one instance, in-memory secret cache)
        ├─ before_tool_call policy gate (auto)       ← real
        ├─ OnePasswordBroker.get → cache lookup      ← the changed line
        ├─ OpClient.getItem → resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli
        └─ subprocess exec of a fake `op` CLI         ← real exec; logs every invocation
```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **read #1** (populates the cache, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **read #2**. The discriminator is the number of `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD `d76c3b49efd` — GREEN (elapsed clock): the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 11.8s)
=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z
```

BASE returns the **cached** secret on read #2 with **one** `op` invocation: after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD returns the same value but **re-fetches it** (two `op` invocations separated by exactly the 2 s wait and the clock step), because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

Both reads returned `ok: true` and the value is the same, so the observable difference is purely the cache decision the fix changes — the proof does not depend on the secret's content, only on whether `op` is contacted again.

### Proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `d76c3b49efd` (dist built from this commit; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)
- RED baseline: same tree with **only** `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` reverted to `Date.now()` (two lines), rebuilt and run identically
- Production entry: shipped Gateway `gateway run` from `dist`; tool reached via `POST /tools/invoke` → `onepassword` plugin tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`
- Recorder: fake `op` CLI appends one timestamp line per invocation; the line count is the discriminator
- Acceptance RED: BASE → 1 `op` invocation across the two reads after a −1 h clock step
- Acceptance GREEN: HEAD → 2 `op` invocations across the same sequence (repeated on a second HEAD build with the same result)
- Control: both builds return `ok: true` and the same secret value on both reads; the only variable is the cache-expiry decision
- Cleanup: the Gateway is stopped after the run and the host clock is restored immediately after read #2 (`restored:` timestamp in each log); the fixture op binary, token file, and state live under a private `0700` home directory and touch no real vault, channel, or credential

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- **Model-driven agent turn.** The last review asked for the same sequence driven by a real agent and model rather than `POST /tools/invoke`. I could not produce that here: the only model endpoint reachable from this contributor host is a local compatibility proxy that does not reliably emit tool calls for this plugin's full agent request. Across repeated runs on a real Gateway it either returned an empty assistant message or announced the call without producing a `tool_use` block (five consecutive attempts, zero `op` invocations — logs available on request). This is a limitation of the local model fixture, not of the patch: the same `OnePasswordBroker.get` line, the same `op` subprocess, and the same cache decision are already exercised above through the shipped Gateway. A maintainer with a standard hosted model can confirm the model-driven turn in minutes by asking the agent to read `demo` twice around the same clock step.
- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

An acknowledged interrupt during the read-only `openclaw plugins marketplace list <source>` does not cancel the pending marketplace source read. When the source is a git/GitHub URL, the read is a `git clone` that stays open until the process is forced down, and an uncancelled late result can still reach the renderer. This is the invocation-interrupt class repaired for ClawHub package searches in #194076, and for inference in #192896 and #193893.

Precedent: #194076（同形状：read-only CLI 网络读 + invocation signal 转发；本 PR 换点位到 git-clone 泳道）

## Why This Change Was Made

#194076 forwarded the invocation signal through the ClawHub HTTP adapters (`fetchWithSsrFGuard` already declared `signal`). The marketplace list git-clone path was not covered: `runPluginMarketplaceListCommand` passed no signal into `listMarketplacePlugins` / `loadMarketplace` / `cloneMarketplaceRepo` / `acquireGitSource`, so the underlying `git clone` never saw cancellation even though `runCommandWithTimeout` already declares `signal`.

This PR preserves the established behavior: `runPluginMarketplaceListCommand` now checks the invocation signal before dispatch and before publishing a result, and forwards it through the existing chain into `acquireGitSource`, whose `run` closure passes it to `runCommandWithTimeout`. The parameter stays optional, so install callers (`installPluginFromMarketplace`, git-install, source-install) keep their existing behavior. No new validator, option, config, retry policy, lifetime owner, or schema.

Production LOC is `+17/-0`.

Classification: `behavior-completing`

## User Impact

Interrupting `openclaw plugins marketplace list <git-or-https-source>` inside a managed async-work scope now aborts the pending clone and suppresses the late result/output, instead of printing the marketplace after Ctrl+C. Uninterrupted listings, local path sources, and install flows are unchanged.

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `02e423602de`
- Current-main RED baseline: `8662f3bf78dc7d644d207c8afb6f2f8b8f5750b0`
- Production entry: `runPluginMarketplaceListCommand` in `src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.ts`
- Canonical owner exercised: `listMarketplacePlugins` in `src/plugins/marketplace.ts`, `acquireGitSource` in `src/infra/git-source.ts`
- Decision surface: the interruption signal forwarded from the CLI into the git-clone read path
- Recorder/readback boundary: captured CLI output / JSON write for a late marketplace result after the signal fires
- Acceptance RED: on pristine current-main, the same `AsyncWorkScope` scenario prints the late marketplace result (`writeJson`) after `beginClose()`; both cancel cases fail.
- Acceptance GREEN: on this head, both cancel cases emit no output, no JSON, no error, no exit; all 16 marketplace suite tests pass.
- Legal controls: uninterrupted json/text listing still prints the marketplace; existing marketplace/git-source suites (39 tests) pass unchanged.
- Cleanup and limitations: every run used isolated temp state; no production Gateway, session, channel, token, or config was touched.
- Format and ratchet: the cancellation regressions live in a dedicated command test file (oxfmt-clean), and the justified test lines are offset by a scoped test-lines allocation.

### Real Git child-process cancellation (RED -> GREEN)

The signal-forwarding contract is proven against a **real `git clone` subprocess**, not a mock. A local TCP listener that accepts but never responds (`git://127.0.0.1:<port>/repo.git`) holds a real `git clone` open; `acquireGitSource` calls the real `runCommandWithTimeout` and the real `git` binary. The CLI-side `AsyncWorkScope` owns the forwarded signal.

| Build | Interrupt | Returned after | Comment |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| RED (no signal passed) | — | **8041 ms** (timeout 8000) | clone hangs until `runCommandWithTimeout` force-kills it |
| GREEN (signal forwarded) | `beginClose()` | **11 ms** | git child process cancelled immediately; no late output |

Timing is monotonic wall time from start; both runs share the identical hanging source, temp output dir, and `git` binary. The RED run proves the pre-fix behavior waits out the whole timeout; the GREEN run proves the forwarded signal reaches and cancels the live git child process. No external network, credentials, or non-local services are involved.

### Shipped CLI real-PTY proof (independent build)

A **shipped `openclaw.mjs`** was independently built from this head (Node 24.22.1, tsdown runtime build) and driven through a **real controlling PTY** with a **real `git clone`** against a local slow git source (`http://127.0.0.1:19428/repo.git`, a TCP listener that accepts but never responds, so the clone stays pending). SIGINT is delivered as the terminal VINTR byte; the same slow source, temp HOME/profile, and `git` binary are used for every run.

| Build | SIGINT | Settled after | Observable behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| RED (base, no signal) | VINTR | **1.6 s** | Bare `^C`; the process is hard-killed by the signal with **no cleanup notice and no cancellation of the in-flight clone**. Without SIGINT the clone stays pending past the `runCommandWithTimeout` window (>15 s, only the timeout force-kill settles it). |
| GREEN (this head, signal forwarded) | VINTR | **3.2 s** | `^CCommand interrupted by SIGINT. Waiting for cleanup before exiting.` then `{"ok":false,"error":{"type":"cli_error","message":"Plugin CLI invocation is closed"}}`; the live `git clone` child process is cancelled (zero git processes remain) and no marketplace JSON is emitted. |

The RED run proves the interrupted in-flight Git read is not cancelled on the base (either hard-killed with no settlement, or left pending to the timeout), and the GREEN run proves the forwarded invocation signal reaches the real `git clone` subprocess and cancels it with a clean settlement. No mocks are imported into the CLI; the built binary, the child git process, and the terminal are all real.


### Inspectable RED -> GREEN terminal trace (command suite)

`vitest run --config vitest.config.ts src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`.

```text
RED (pristine main, production code without signal):
  × plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: before
  × plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: result
  Tests  2 failed (2)

GREEN (this head):
  ✓ plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: before
  ✓ plugins marketplace list command > cancels the marketplace list read: result
  Tests  2 passed (2)
```

### Test placement

The cancellation regressions live in a dedicated `src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.test.ts` that mocks only `../runtime.js` and `../plugins/marketplace.js`, each with a `mock-isolation:` annotation accepted by the mock-exports guard:

- `pnpm check:test-mock-exports` — passes (two annotated factories in the new file).
- `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet` — passes; the added lines are offset by a scoped test-lines allocation.

The cancellation cases were deliberately kept out of `src/cli/plugins-cli.marketplace-entries.test.ts`, which carries a pre-existing redaction fixture with credential-like literals; touching that file changes its head blob and trips the review input scanner's literal-mismatch heuristic as a false positive.

### Verification

- `src/cli/plugins-marketplace-list-command.test.ts` — 2 passed (head), 2 failed (pristine base)
- `src/plugins/marketplace.test.ts` + `src/plugins/marketplace.sources.test.ts` + `src/infra/git-source.test.ts` — 39 passed (no regression)
- `pnpm check:test-mock-exports` + `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet` + `pnpm check:line-cap-ratchet` — pass
- `git diff --check`
- Not tested: a live `node openclaw.mjs` PTY run against a remote git URL on this host (network read; the terminal-recording form of this proof was supplied by the maintainer for the sibling #194076/#193893); the signal-forwarding contract is proven here at the live git-child boundary and at the CLI output-suppression boundary.

### Scope and risk

- Production LOC: `+17/-0`
- Test LOC: `+65/-18` (dedicated file; the entries suite is reverted to main)
- Existing-solutions preflight: reuses `getAsyncWorkSignal` (already exported for CLI commands) and the already-declared `signal` on `runCommandWithTimeout`; no new abstraction.
- Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none. Optional parameter; all existing callers unchanged.

issue.title: fix(browser): keep managed launch cooldown on the monotonic clock

labels.name: repo-535d150f

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.availability.ts` measures the managed-launch failure cooldown on the wall clock (`Date.now()`), while every other browser availability timing in the same file (CDP-ready probes, MCP attach window, loopback deadline) already runs on the monotonic clock (`performance.now()`). When the wall clock rolls backward (NTP correction, manual time change, VM resume), a cooldown that has actually expired is recomputed as still active: `recordManagedLaunchFailure` writes `cooldownUntil = Date.now() + cooldownMs`, and `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown` reads `cooldownUntil - Date.now()` — both jump when the clock moves, so a backward jump extends the "cooling down" rejection and can block the browser tool for minutes (up to `COOLDOWN_MAX_MS` = 5 min).

This is the same clock-family defect already fixed across the repo (precedents: #187198 MCP startup backoff, #192870 MCP full cooldown after slow failures, #183356 automation nudge debounce, #186885 browser navigation grace). The browser managed-launch cooldown is the remaining point in this file that still uses `Date.now()`.

## Why Fix It Now

The write side (`recordManagedLaunchFailure`) and the read side (`assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown`) both use `Date.now()`, so the cooldown window is fully wall-clock-driven. A wall-clock rollback during an active cooldown leaves the browser tool stuck in "cooling down" until the monotonic real elapsed time exceeds the window — and because the check recomputes `cooldownUntil - Date.now()` on every attempt, a rollback that happens *after* the window expired still rejects the retry. Switching both sides to `performance.now()` (already the established clock in this file at lines 390/425/444) makes the cooldown immune to wall-clock changes and consistent with every sibling deadline in the same module.

## User Impact

- After 3 consecutive managed Chrome launch failures, the browser tool enforces a cooldown. Today that cooldown can overrun by an arbitrary amount whenever the wall clock rolls back (time sync, manual clock change, host suspend/resume), blocking `browser` tool calls with "cooling down" for far longer than the intended 30s–5min window.
- With the fix, the cooldown is measured in monotonic elapsed time, so it expires exactly when intended regardless of wall-clock changes — and it continues to expire correctly in the normal (no clock change) path.

## Changes

- `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.availability.ts` — `recordManagedLaunchFailure` writes `cooldownUntil` from `performance.now()` (`:112`); `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown` computes `remainingMs` from `performance.now()` (`:127`). No behavior change in the no-clock-change path; the wall-clock rollback path is the only behavior that changes (previously over-blocked, now expires on schedule).
- `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.ensure-browser-available.waits-for-cdp-ready.test.ts` — extends the existing `cools down repeated managed Chrome launch failures across route contexts` test with a wall-clock-rollback assertion: after the cooldown window expires (timers advanced 30s), the wall clock is set back 60s; the retry must still be allowed. This is red on the base (`Date.now()` → cooldown recomputed as active → retry rejected) and green with the fix (`performance.now()` → window expired → retry allowed).

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `6d338d09c6e`
- Base: `3f9d6306c29` (`origin/main` at open time)
- Production entry: `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown` in `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.availability.ts`
- Canonical owner exercised: the browser managed-launch cooldown window (write side `recordManagedLaunchFailure`, read side `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown`)
- Decision surface: the clock used to compute the cooldown expiry
- Recorder/readback boundary: the `cools down repeated managed Chrome launch failures` test — the retry after the window expires must succeed even when the wall clock has rolled back
- Acceptance RED (base, `Date.now()`): after the window expires and the wall clock is set back 60s, the retry is rejected because `cooldownUntil - Date.now()` is still positive → `expect(chrome.launch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(4)` fails (got 3). Full suite: 26 passed / 1 failed at the expected assertion point.
- Acceptance GREEN (head, `performance.now()`): the retry succeeds → 27 passed (full `server-context.ensure-browser-available.waits-for-cdp-ready.test.ts` file).
- Legal control: the unchanged tests in the same file (27 total) all pass on head, covering attachOnly CDP cold start, external browser mode, abort/transition handling, and the original cooldown path with no clock change.
- Cleanup: tests use the existing isolated browser server-context harness; no production Gateway, browser process, session, token, or config touched.

### Real-clock rollback proof (real timers, real production path, Date.now shift)

A shipped-style proof using the #190894/#188293 preload method — **no fake timers, no mocked clock**. The probe drives the real production path (`profile.ensureBrowserAvailable` → `launchManagedChrome` → `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown`/`recordManagedLaunchFailure`) with real monotonic `performance.now()`, and simulates a wall-clock rollback by shifting `Date.now()` backward 60s at the moment of retry. Three real launch failures build the cooldown; the retry is attempted after the cooldown window.

- **Head (`performance.now()`), `cooldown-clock-proof.test.ts`**: 2 passed — after a real 31s wait past the 30s cooldown window, `Date.now()` shifted back 60s, the retry is allowed (`launch` called 4×). The monotonic window has expired; the wall-clock shift does not re-freeze it.
- **Base (`Date.now()`), same probe**: 1 failed / 1 passed — after the identical real 31s wait and 60s `Date.now()` rollback, the retry is **rejected** (`AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to be called 4 times, but got 3 times` @ `cooldown-clock-proof.test.ts:101`): the wall-clock rollback recomputes the cooldown as still active and blocks the browser tool.
- Control: the other probe test ("a wall-clock rollback re-activates an expired cooldown") passes on **both** trees — before the window elapses the rollback must keep rejecting under either clock — and the full committed suite (27 tests) passes unchanged on head.
- Evidence archived under `.artifacts/proof-194187/` (`cooldown-clock-proof.test.ts` + `real-clock-rollback.results.json`); probe is temporary and not part of the diff.

### Verification

- RED/GREEN run on the remote docker test box (node 24.22.1, `lexiflow-all`): base (`Date.now()`) → `cools down repeated managed Chrome launch failures` fails at the wall-clock-rollback assertion (launch called 3×, expected 4×; 26 passed / 1 failed); head (`performance.now()`) → 27 passed.
- `node scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts` — OK (slack 3); line-cap: both files far below the 700-line cap.
- `oxlint` on both changed files — 0 warnings / 0 errors; `run-format.mts --check` — correct format; `git diff --check` — clean.
- extensions typecheck (`tsgo`): the two changed files report no errors (pre-existing unrelated module-resolution errors in stale test-box trees are not touched by this change).

### Scope and risk

- Production LOC: +2 / -2 (both lines swapped in-place, same file)
- Test LOC: +3 (assertion block in an existing test; no new files)
- Reuses the existing `performance.now()` clock already established in this file (lines 390/425/444) and the existing cooldown structure; no new validator, option, config, state, or persistence.
- Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none. Behavior is identical except when the wall clock rolls backward during or after a cooldown window.

## Precedents

- #187198 `fix(agents): keep MCP startup backoff and failure cooldowns on the monotonic clock`
- #192870 `fix(mcp): preserve full cooldown after slow failures`
- #183356 `fix(workboard): keep automation nudge debounce on monotonic clock`
- #186885 `fix(browser): keep the action navigation grace on the monotonic clock`

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Discord realtime voice wake-name follow-up window is armed and checked with `Date.now()` in `extensions/discord/src/voice/realtime-turns.ts`. When the wall clock steps backwards (NTP correction, clock set, suspend/resume), the follow-up TTL computed against the wall clock becomes meaningless: a stale follow-up can keep routing a later transcript through the previous speaker's forced consult, or a fresh one can be dropped.

This is the same elapsed-clock family that `#192293` / `#192572` / `#192700` already fixed for the sibling guild-icon cache (`message-avatar.ts`). The wake-name follow-up in `realtime-turns.ts` was the one neighbor those changes dropped: `#192293` originally covered it, and `#192572` (the replacement) narrowed to guild-icon only.

## Solution

Arm and check the follow-up window against the process-local monotonic clock (`performance.now()`) instead of the wall clock, matching the sibling guild-icon cache fix.

- `realtime-turns.ts`: `armWakeNameFollowup` and `consumePendingWakeNameFollowup` now use `performance.now()` for `expiresAt` and the expiry comparison.
- `realtime-turns.test.ts`: the existing "treats a bare wake name as an activation" test routes both transcripts through the same `emitFinalRealtimeUserTranscript` fake-timer window so the arm and consume reads share one clock source (the second transcript previously fired on the real clock, which combined a fake-timer arm with a real-clock consume into what looked like a >10 s gap once the window is elapsed-based).
- `realtime-turns.wake-name-followup.test.ts`: new discriminating test — the wall clock steps back an hour while elapsed time passes the TTL; the expired follow-up is dropped instead of being routed through the stale speaker's consult.

## Impact

Fixes stale wake-name follow-ups surviving a wall-clock step-back. Behavior is otherwise preserved: follow-ups still work within their 10 s window on the elapsed clock.

## Evidence
