issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.availability.ts` measures the managed-launch failure cooldown on the wall clock (`Date.now()`), while every other browser availability timing in the same file (CDP-ready probes, MCP attach window, loopback deadline) already runs on the monotonic clock (`performance.now()`). When the wall clock rolls backward (NTP correction, manual time change, VM resume), a cooldown that has actually expired is recomputed as still active: `recordManagedLaunchFailure` writes `cooldownUntil = Date.now() + cooldownMs`, and `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown` reads `cooldownUntil - Date.now()` — both jump when the clock moves, so a backward jump extends the "cooling down" rejection and can block the browser tool for minutes (up to `COOLDOWN_MAX_MS` = 5 min).

This is the same clock-family defect already fixed across the repo (precedents: #187198 MCP startup backoff, #192870 MCP full cooldown after slow failures, #183356 automation nudge debounce, #186885 browser navigation grace). The browser managed-launch cooldown is the remaining point in this file that still uses `Date.now()`.

## Why Fix It Now

The write side (`recordManagedLaunchFailure`) and the read side (`assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown`) both use `Date.now()`, so the cooldown window is fully wall-clock-driven. A wall-clock rollback during an active cooldown leaves the browser tool stuck in "cooling down" until the monotonic real elapsed time exceeds the window — and because the check recomputes `cooldownUntil - Date.now()` on every attempt, a rollback that happens *after* the window expired still rejects the retry. Switching both sides to `performance.now()` (already the established clock in this file at lines 390/425/444) makes the cooldown immune to wall-clock changes and consistent with every sibling deadline in the same module.

## User Impact

- After 3 consecutive managed Chrome launch failures, the browser tool enforces a cooldown. Today that cooldown can overrun by an arbitrary amount whenever the wall clock rolls back (time sync, manual clock change, host suspend/resume), blocking `browser` tool calls with "cooling down" for far longer than the intended 30s–5min window.
- With the fix, the cooldown is measured in monotonic elapsed time, so it expires exactly when intended regardless of wall-clock changes — and it continues to expire correctly in the normal (no clock change) path.

## Changes

- `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.availability.ts` — `recordManagedLaunchFailure` writes `cooldownUntil` from `performance.now()` (`:112`); `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown` computes `remainingMs` from `performance.now()` (`:127`). No behavior change in the no-clock-change path; the wall-clock rollback path is the only behavior that changes (previously over-blocked, now expires on schedule).
- `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.ensure-browser-available.waits-for-cdp-ready.test.ts` — extends the existing `cools down repeated managed Chrome launch failures across route contexts` test with a wall-clock-rollback assertion: after the cooldown window expires (timers advanced 30s), the wall clock is set back 60s; the retry must still be allowed. This is red on the base (`Date.now()` → cooldown recomputed as active → retry rejected) and green with the fix (`performance.now()` → window expired → retry allowed).

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `6d338d09c6e`
- Base: `3f9d6306c29` (`origin/main` at open time)
- Production entry: `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown` in `extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.availability.ts`
- Canonical owner exercised: the browser managed-launch cooldown window (write side `recordManagedLaunchFailure`, read side `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown`)
- Decision surface: the clock used to compute the cooldown expiry
- Recorder/readback boundary: the `cools down repeated managed Chrome launch failures` test — the retry after the window expires must succeed even when the wall clock has rolled back
- Acceptance RED (base, `Date.now()`): after the window expires and the wall clock is set back 60s, the retry is rejected because `cooldownUntil - Date.now()` is still positive → `expect(chrome.launch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(4)` fails (got 3). Full suite: 26 passed / 1 failed at the expected assertion point.
- Acceptance GREEN (head, `performance.now()`): the retry succeeds → 27 passed (full `server-context.ensure-browser-available.waits-for-cdp-ready.test.ts` file).
- Legal control: the unchanged tests in the same file (27 total) all pass on head, covering attachOnly CDP cold start, external browser mode, abort/transition handling, and the original cooldown path with no clock change.
- Cleanup: tests use the existing isolated browser server-context harness; no production Gateway, browser process, session, token, or config touched.

### Real-clock rollback proof (real timers, real production path, Date.now shift)

A shipped-style proof using the #190894/#188293 preload method — **no fake timers, no mocked clock**. The probe drives the real production path (`profile.ensureBrowserAvailable` → `launchManagedChrome` → `assertManagedLaunchNotCoolingDown`/`recordManagedLaunchFailure`) with real monotonic `performance.now()`, and simulates a wall-clock rollback by shifting `Date.now()` backward 60s at the moment of retry. Three real launch failures build the cooldown; the retry is attempted after the cooldown window.

- **Head (`performance.now()`), `cooldown-clock-proof.test.ts`**: 2 passed — after a real 31s wait past the 30s cooldown window, `Date.now()` shifted back 60s, the retry is allowed (`launch` called 4×). The monotonic window has expired; the wall-clock shift does not re-freeze it.
- **Base (`Date.now()`), same probe**: 1 failed / 1 passed — after the identical real 31s wait and 60s `Date.now()` rollback, the retry is **rejected** (`AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to be called 4 times, but got 3 times` @ `cooldown-clock-proof.test.ts:101`): the wall-clock rollback recomputes the cooldown as still active and blocks the browser tool.
- Control: the other probe test ("a wall-clock rollback re-activates an expired cooldown") passes on **both** trees — before the window elapses the rollback must keep rejecting under either clock — and the full committed suite (27 tests) passes unchanged on head.
- Evidence archived under `.artifacts/proof-194187/` (`cooldown-clock-proof.test.ts` + `real-clock-rollback.results.json`); probe is temporary and not part of the diff.

### Verification

- RED/GREEN run on the remote docker test box (node 24.22.1, `lexiflow-all`): base (`Date.now()`) → `cools down repeated managed Chrome launch failures` fails at the wall-clock-rollback assertion (launch called 3×, expected 4×; 26 passed / 1 failed); head (`performance.now()`) → 27 passed.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`resolveSlackChannelMemberIds` (`extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.ts`) caches a channel's member roster for 60 s so each bot-authored room message does not page `conversations.members`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `expiresAtMs >= Date.now()`
- completed roster: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + CHANNEL_MEMBERS_CACHE_TTL_MS`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host (NTP correction, VM resume, manual `date`) keeps a roster that was written before the step fresh for the length of the step. Members added later are missing from the cached set, which feeds channel-authorization decisions, so a newly added operator can stay unauthorized until the step elapses.

## Why This Change Was Made

Expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`accountId` + optional team scope + channel), 512-entry cap, in-flight coalescing, and the "delete the pending promise if it is still the latest" cleanup are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer pins a stale roster. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cached roster, same Slack API calls.

## Evidence

Regression test run through the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached channel members on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — still one `conversations.members` call after the step | PASS |
| `reuses cached channel members` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

HEAD output:

```
 ✓ extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

The new test steps only the process-local clock and advances fake timers past the TTL, then asserts a second `conversations.members` call — a passing result requires the pre-step entry to be treated as expired while the wall clock reads an hour earlier.

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.ts:108` | Freshness read and pending-entry write only |
| `extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.ts:133` | Completed-roster write only; cap and coalescing unchanged |

### Real-behavior proof ceiling (requesting maintainer help)

ClawSweeper asks for a final-effect proof on the running Slack Gateway path: owner arrival permits bot turns and owner removal prevents agent dispatch after roster expiry under a backward clock step. That evidence is **structurally unreachable here** as a contributor:

- No Slack workspace bot token on this Linux host, so a live `conversations.members` round-trip through the shipped `resolveSlackChannelMemberIds` cannot be recorded.
- ClawSweeper has also flagged this item `clawsweeper-verdict:needs-human` / `hold=security` (it is a security-boundary decision because the roster gates bot-message admission). A held security item is a maintainer judgment, not something contributor proof clears on its own.

The direction matters and is the reason this is security-relevant: with a stale roster pinned by a backward clock step, an **owner removed from the channel can keep authorizing bot turns** past the intended 60-second window (`authorizeSlackBotRoomMessage` reads the cached roster before any fresh membership check). The committed regression asserts the roster is re-fetched after the TTL despite the backward step (red on BASE, green on HEAD), but the final-effect (blocked agent dispatch) needs the live path.

This is one of a family of identical elapsed-clock fixes (#193412, #193392, #193397, #193410); #193412 and #193392 carry real-boundary proof where the transport allowed it. If a maintainer can run the shipped Slack path under a backward clock step with a test workspace, or can decide based on the family precedent, we will act on the result.

### Not tested

- No real clock step on a running Gateway; the test steps the process-local clock only.
- No live Slack `conversations.members` call (needs a workspace bot token); the client is mocked at the `ctx.app.client` boundary.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no production Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one extension module plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen); treating the roster as authorization authority (it already is only one input — `cache.delete` on expiry keeps the same trust model).

Scope: `extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.ts` and its test file.

</details>

The regression stays useful if a maintainer wants to pick up the elapsed-clock direction; body and comments document the proof ceiling and the family precedent (#193412, #193392 carry real-boundary proof where the transport allowed it).

issue.body:
Closes #184409

## What Problem This Solves

When a loopback client fails an `operator.*` scope check, the only signal in the logs is a bare `missing scope: operator.read` error. Nothing in the connect record records *why* the client was not considered local. In the reported incident, a host-level `POSTROUTING MASQUERADE` rule rewrote the source address of loopback connections, so the gateway legitimately resolved `pairingLocality = "remote"` — the scope logic was correct, but the observability was not, and several hours were spent hunting an authorization bug that was actually networking.

The gateway already computes `pairingLocality` (`direct_local` / `cli_container_local` / `shared_secret_loopback_local` / `browser_container_local` / `remote`) and already logs the peer address as `remote=`. The connect journal line omits only the locality decision.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `client connected` control-log record in `attachGatewayWsConnectionSession` (`src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-session.ts`) now emits one additional segment, `locality=${pairingLocality}`, using the value already resolved earlier in the same function. No new collection, persistence, RPC, config, or grants change; the authorization boundary is untouched, matching the ClawSweeper recommendation on the issue: *"Approve diagnostics only: Expose the resolved locality in the existing connection record, retain the existing peer-address field, and validate local and remote connection logging without changing grants."* The optional NAT-locality proposal is explicitly out of scope.

Production LOC is `+1/-0`.

Classification: `behavior-preserving` (the connect journal line gains one segment; all existing segments are unchanged and the peer-address field is retained).

## User Impact

Operators troubleshooting `missing scope` denials on hosts with NAT/MASQUERADE rules now see the resolved locality directly in the connect journal line, e.g. `client connected conn=… remote=172.22.219.216 locality=remote`, making this class of problem self-diagnosing. Deployments without address rewriting see `locality=direct_local` (or the applicable locality) with no other change. Log parsers that key on the existing segments keep working because every existing segment is preserved.

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `613fc683cd2b017a76508b9149b09beb2affbf41`

- Canonical owner exercised: `attachGatewayWsConnectionSession` in `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/connect-session.ts`
- Decision surface: the `client connected` control-log line recorded via `logWsControl.info`.
- Recorder/readback boundary: the recorded journal string segments (`conn=`, `remote=`, `locality=`).
- Acceptance RED: on the current-main file content (md5 `d6261060c9fc46b012e6741cee58f59a`, identical at `2ce21647d` and `3bf38f7722`), the new test fails at the expected assertion — the recorded line is `client connected conn=conn-locality-local client=gateway-client name=gateway-client mode=backend role=operator auth=none version=dev platform=test build=legacy remote=127.0.0.1` with no `locality=` segment.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for this exact head** (`d76c3b49efd`, and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read) as a long-running Gateway, and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z

## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Discord realtime voice wake-name follow-up window is armed and checked with `Date.now()` in `extensions/discord/src/voice/realtime-turns.ts`. When the wall clock steps backwards (NTP correction, clock set, suspend/resume), the follow-up TTL computed against the wall clock becomes meaningless: a stale follow-up can keep routing a later transcript through the previous speaker's forced consult, or a fresh one can be dropped.

This is the same elapsed-clock family that `#192293` / `#192572` / `#192700` already fixed for the sibling guild-icon cache (`message-avatar.ts`). The wake-name follow-up in `realtime-turns.ts` was the one neighbor those changes dropped: `#192293` originally covered it, and `#192572` (the replacement) narrowed to guild-icon only.

## Solution

Arm and check the follow-up window against the process-local monotonic clock (`performance.now()`) instead of the wall clock, matching the sibling guild-icon cache fix.

- `realtime-turns.ts`: `armWakeNameFollowup` and `consumePendingWakeNameFollowup` now use `performance.now()` for `expiresAt` and the expiry comparison.
- `realtime-turns.test.ts`: the existing "treats a bare wake name as an activation" test routes both transcripts through the same `emitFinalRealtimeUserTranscript` fake-timer window so the arm and consume reads share one clock source (the second transcript previously fired on the real clock, which combined a fake-timer arm with a real-clock consume into what looked like a >10 s gap once the window is elapsed-based).
- `realtime-turns.wake-name-followup.test.ts`: new discriminating test — the wall clock steps back an hour while elapsed time passes the TTL; the expired follow-up is dropped instead of being routed through the stale speaker's consult.

## Impact

Fixes stale wake-name follow-ups surviving a wall-clock step-back. Behavior is otherwise preserved: follow-ups still work within their 10 s window on the elapsed clock.

## Evidence

Red/green on the new test, run in the discord voice vitest environment (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/discord/src/voice/realtime-turns.wake-name-followup.test.ts`):

- **Base** (`Date.now()`): `drops an expired wake-name follow-up after the wall clock steps backwards` fails — `expected "vi.fn()" to not be called at all, but actually been called 1 times` (the stale follow-up is mis-accepted and the agent is consulted).
- **Head** (`performance.now()`): same test passes; the expired follow-up is dropped and the agent is not called.

Full discord voice suite green on head: 53 test files, 668 tests passed.

Precedent: #192700 (elapsed clock for Discord caches), #192572, #192293.

There is no Discord API surface that exposes it: a live voice-session trace would have to make a real host clock jump backwards (NTP correction, `clock_settime`, suspend/resume) while two wake-name transcripts land 11 s apart in the same realtime bridge session — neither the clock step nor the TTL boundary is drivable from a live Discord bot without root on the host, and no CI runner hosts a Discord voice channel.

The strongest proof reachable here is what the PR already carries: production voice owners (`DiscordVoiceManager` → `realtime-speaker-session` → `DiscordRealtimeTurns` → `onAcceptedTranscript` → `agentCommand`) exercised end to end through the in-process harness with only the Discord gateway, realtime bridge transport, and agent boundary mocked. Red/green is discriminating: on base (`Date.now()`) the backward-clock case fails with the follow-up mis-accepted (agent consulted), on head (`performance.now()`) it passes and the expired follow-up is dropped.

Remote onboarding rebuilds a discovered Gateway's direct URL from a bare host, dropping IPv6 brackets that the discovery target already knows how to add. It suggests an unparseable authority such as `wss://2001:db8::1:18789`; the connection-method label and trust prompt lose the brackets too.

The fix reuses the existing `formatHostForUrl` helper once as `hostLabel`, following sibling discovery consumers and #190942, rather than adding another formatter or validator. issue.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A backward wall-clock adjustment keeps live provider catalog entries alive past their configured TTL, so a repeated discovery reuses the stale upstream metadata/document instead of refreshing it.

`src/plugins/provider-live-catalog-cache.ts` measured freshness against `Date.now()`:

- `getCachedLiveCatalogValue` compared `entry.expiresAt > rawNow`, with `expiresAt` stamped from the wall clock.
- `armLiveCatalogExpiry` / `expireLiveCatalogs` scheduled and swept on the wall clock.

After a backwards step, an entry stays "fresh" for the length of the step. The shared upstream metadata feed (`getCachedUpstreamProviderCatalog`, 300 s TTL) is the directly affected document.

## Why This Change Was Made

Expiry now runs on `monotonicNow()` (`src/shared/monotonic-time.ts`), matching the elapsed-clock caches in core and extensions (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193358).

**The published deadline stays on the wall clock.** `consumeLiveCatalog` forwards the entry deadline through `recordLiveCatalogExpiry` to `providerExpiries`, and `src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.catalog-access.ts:581` filters providers with `expiresAt <= Date.now()`. So the entry carries two fields:

- `expiresAt` — elapsed deadline, owns cache freshness and the sweep.
- `publishedExpiresAt` — wall-clock deadline, still published to catalog expiries.
- `publishedNow` — selects the clock for `publishedExpiresAt` so the `now` test hook keeps driving both.

Precedent: #192700 (`fix: use elapsed time for caches and chat recovery windows`), #193147 (`fix(runtime): expire discovery and room caches on elapsed time`), #191606 (`fix(cache): keep private cache TTLs on elapsed time`), #193358 (`fix(active-memory): expire recall cache on elapsed time`).

## Shipped route (addressing the #193358 exclusion)

#193358 landed the elapsed-cache family without this PR because "the exercised shipped inventory route either uses the static catalog or explicitly bypasses this cache during refresh". The static-catalog half holds; the bypass half does not, for OpenCode Zen and OpenCode Go:

- `extensions/opencode/provider-catalog.ts:73` and `extensions/opencode-go/provider-catalog.ts:83` both set `metadataEndpoint` to `https://models.opencode.ai/api.json`.
- `extensions/opencode/index.ts:144` and `extensions/opencode-go/index.ts:80` run the live branch from `catalog.run` → `buildOpencodeZenLiveProviderConfig` / `buildOpencodeGoLiveProviderConfig` → `buildLiveProvider` (`src/plugin-sdk/provider-catalog-live-runtime.ts:355`) → `refreshMetadata` → `getCachedUpstreamProviderCatalog` → `getCachedLiveCatalogValue` with `keyParts: ["upstream-provider-catalog", endpoint]` and a 300 s TTL. This matches `docs/plugins/sdk-provider-plugins/model-catalogs.md` ("Live builds refresh metadata before deriving static eligibility").
- The refresh bypass only covers the *first* lookup of an acquisition (`consumeLiveCatalogRefresh` consumes the key once). A second metadata lookup inside the same catalog run, and every ordinary (non-refresh) inventory read, takes the cache path.

What is *not* claimed: `prepareOpencodeZenModel` (`extensions/opencode/provider-catalog.ts:96`) really does call `refreshMetadata` outside `catalog.run` and therefore bypasses the cache, and the host-side caller of `buildLiveProvider` reaches it through `catalog.run` only. The proof below drives the `catalog.run` path, including its cache-hit reads.

## User Impact

With a live OpenCode catalog feed, an expired entry refreshes after its elapsed TTL even when the host clock moves backward. Warm entries still reuse the cache, the published expiry handed to the catalog runtime is unchanged, and behavior without a clock step is identical. No new setting, error text, public SDK export, stored format, or migration.

## Evidence

Both sides ran on the remote Linux test host (Docker, Node v24.22.1) through the repository entry `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run <path>`. BASE is `origin/main` (`46943d587ac`) archived per side; HEAD is the PR tip. Trees were restored/re-checked per run.

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/plugins/provider-live-catalog-cache.test.ts` — `expires cached catalogs on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | FAIL | PASS |
| `src/plugin-sdk/provider-catalog-live-upstream.test.ts` — `reloads the upstream provider catalog after the wall clock steps backwards` | FAIL | PASS |
| `src/plugin-sdk/provider-catalog-live-runtime.strict.test.ts` (whole file) | PASS | PASS |
| `src/plugin-sdk/provider-catalog-shared{,.refresh,.cancellation}.test.ts` (whole files) | PASS | PASS |

BASE failure (cache test):

```
AssertionError: expected "spy" to be called 2 times, but got 1 times
 ❯ src/plugins/provider-live-catalog-cache.test.ts:92:24
```

BASE failure (upstream test):

```
AssertionError: expected "spy" to be called 2 times, but got 1 times
 ❯ src/plugin-sdk/provider-catalog-live-upstream.test.ts:287:29
```

The clock step is process-local only (`vi.setSystemTime`); the real clock is never touched. Both regression tests step `Date` backwards *and* advance the faked elapsed clock, so they land past the TTL by elapsed time.

**Discovery trace through the shipped `catalog.run` entry (added this revision).** A new regression in `extensions/opencode/index.test.ts` drives `buildOpencodeZenLiveProviderConfig` — the exact run callback `catalog.run` invokes for a configured OpenCode provider (`extensions/opencode/index.ts:149`) — instead of calling the cache loader directly. A `fetchGuard` spy records the upstream metadata download count for `https://models.opencode.ai/api.json`:

| Step | BASE (`Date.now`) | HEAD (`monotonicNow`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First live discovery | metadata download `1` | metadata download `1` |
| Second live discovery inside the 300 s elapsed TTL | `1` (cache hit) | `1` (cache hit) |
| Backwards 1 h wall-clock step + 301 000 elapsed ms | **`1` (stale reuse: deadline stayed "fresh" for the step)** | **`2` (expired by elapsed time; upstream reloaded)** |

BASE fails the third step (`AssertionError: expected 1 to be 2`); HEAD passes. The `fetchGuard` spy records the real metadata URL and a real `RequestInit`, and the fixed `catalog.run` callback path (`runLiveProviderCatalog` → `buildLiveProvider` → `refreshMetadata` → `getCachedUpstreamProviderCatalog`) is unchanged — only the network is substituted, matching the "installed HTTP plugin + local protocol fixture" bar #193358 set.

CI follow-up in this revision: the existing `preserves failure, caches authoritative empty until expiry and supports bypass` test forced expiry with `vi.setSystemTime(1_000)` alone, which no longer moves an elapsed deadline. It now also advances the faked timers by the same span; verified red on `46943d587ac`-equivalent branch state before the test edit and green after (remote run above).

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `src/plugins/provider-live-catalog-cache.ts:17-25,53,63,76,96,116-165` | Expiry/sweep clock only; TTL, keys, caps, pending sharing unchanged |
| `src/plugins/provider-live-catalog-cache.ts:96` | Published wall-clock deadline preserved for `catalog-access.ts:581` |

### Not tested

- No real clock step on a running Gateway; the regression tests step the process-local clock only.
- Not run against a published build.
- Local `pnpm tsgo` cannot run on this contributor host; type checking is left to CI.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow fix in one core cache module plus its tests. If the elapsed-clock direction accepted for the rest of the family applies here, land as-is.

Alternative considered and rejected: a single field with a consumer-side conversion. `catalog-access.ts` compares the published value against `Date.now()` in a different call path with no elapsed baseline, so the two fields are separate facts rather than one transformed one.

</details>

comment.body: Closing as structurally unprovable on this contributor host (see rationale above). The fix itself is sound; the elapsed-clock direction is already approved across the family (#191606/#192700/#193147/#193358).

- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===

2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- **Model-driven agent turn.** The last review asked for the same sequence driven by a real agent and model rather than `POST /tools/invoke`. I could not produce that here: the only model endpoint reachable from this contributor host is a local compatibility proxy that does not reliably emit tool calls for this plugin's full agent request. Across repeated runs on a real Gateway it either returned an empty assistant message or announced the call without producing a `tool_use` block (five consecutive attempts, zero `op` invocations — logs available on request). This is a limitation of the local model fixture, not of the patch: the same `OnePasswordBroker.get` line, the same `op` subprocess, and the same cache decision are already exercised above through the shipped Gateway. A maintainer with a standard hosted model can confirm the model-driven turn in minutes by asking the agent to read `demo` twice around the same clock step.
- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

issue.body:
Fixes #176044

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: realtime Talk input transcription guesses the language per utterance and mishears short phrases ("Yes" → "Ja.", "make the change" → "Make a deal.") when the operator has configured `talk.speechLocale`, because the OpenAI browser session builders never forward that locale to `audio.input.transcription.language`.

## User Impact

User impact: operators who set `talk.speechLocale` now get the same transcription language hint on Control UI/browser realtime Talk sessions that Android already derives from the same setting, so short utterances transcribe in the configured language instead of being auto-detected. Unset, malformed, and unknown locale values behave exactly as before (provider autodetect), and the native/relay paths are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildOpenAIRealtimeGaSessionPolicy` already accepts a `language` parameter and the relay/bridge path already forwards one; only the two browser session builders in `realtime-voice-provider-factory.ts` omitted it. This change resolves the ISO 639-1 component from `talk.speechLocale` once per `createBrowserSession` call and passes it to both builders — no new config option, no SDK/type surface change, no behavior change when the setting is unset. Locale handling mirrors the existing `resolveCallTranscriptionLanguage` precedent in `extensions/voice-call` (PR #190703): BCP-47 → ISO-639-1 via `Intl.Locale`, validated with `Intl.DisplayNames`, underscore form normalized the way the Android Talk config parser does.

## Evidence

**Base** `ab4074fb57e344ccf9ee3ae4f370b6642db374e4` → **Candidate** `447c588446762d9260b0bd1d7628cc0961b9bf65` (branch `fix/openai-talk-speech-locale-transcription`).

Red/green proof — new parameterized cases run against both refs (secretless, Node v24.22.1):

| Case (`talk.speechLocale`) | Expected `transcription.language` | Base | Candidate |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cs-CZ` (GA branch) | `cs` | ❌ red | ✅ green |
| `de_DE` (GA branch, underscore form) | `de` | ❌ red | ✅ green |
| `en` (GA branch) | `en` | ❌ red | ✅ green |
| `xx` (GA branch, unknown) | absent | ✅ | ✅ |
| unset (GA branch) | absent | ✅ | ✅ |
| `cs-CZ` (WebRTC branch) | `cs` | ❌ red | ✅ green |
| `en_US` (WebRTC branch) | `en` | ❌ red | ✅ green |
| `xx` / unset (WebRTC branch) | absent | ✅ | ✅ |

On base: 5 positive cases fail (missing `language`), all negative cases pass — confirming the defect and that the unset path is behaviorally unchanged by the fix. With the candidate: **64/64 tests pass** across the two touched test files.

Checks (all run in the isolated worktree on the pinned toolchain):

```
